hops.title: The banded krait behind the receptor map
hops.text: The receptor tag in that time-lapse was a snake-venom protein carrying a fluorescent dye. In 1963, in a poorly funded, under-equipped pharmacology lab at National Taiwan University during Taiwan's lean post-war years, Chang and Lee separated the venom of the Taiwan banded krait, a black-and-white striped snake, into its neurotoxins. One of them, alpha-bungarotoxin, binds muscle acetylcholine receptors so tightly that it practically never lets go. Other labs used it to isolate the receptor protein, it helped show that antibodies against these receptors cause a common form of myasthenia gravis, and with a dye attached it paints the receptor map beneath two competing axons.

hops.title: Why "use it or lose it" is only half right
hops.text: Developing circuits are often summed up as "use it or lose it," as if a quiet input simply fades. Vision says the comparison matters more. In young mice at the peak of the critical period, four days with one eye closed shifted visual cortical responses toward the open eye as much as longer closures did. Closing both eyes for four days left most responses near normal. Children treated for dense early cataracts fit the pattern: an eye deprived on its own ended up with a narrower visual field than eyes deprived in pairs. One treatment for amblyopia patches the stronger eye so the weaker eye does more of the work.

sources.citation: Gordon JA, Stryker MP. J Neurosci 16(10):3274-3286 (1996), PMID: 8627365.
Bowering ER, Maurer D, Lewis TL, Brent HP. J Pediatr Ophthalmol Strabismus 34(6):347-356 (1997), PMID: 9430061.
Kaur S, Sharda S, Aggarwal H, Dadeya S. Indian J Ophthalmol 71(7):2677-2686 (2023), PMID: 37417105.

hops.afterHeading: A similar contest in the brain
hops.title: Misplaced climbing-fiber synapses and essential tremor
hops.text: Essential tremor is a shake that shows up when the hands move, such as reaching for a cup of coffee. In 2020, Pan, Kuo and colleagues examined postmortem cerebellums from people with the condition and found unusually many climbing-fiber synapses on distal Purkinje-cell dendrites, alongside lower levels of a glutamate receptor protein involved in pruning. Mice short of that protein had a climbing-fiber pruning deficit, excess cerebellar rhythms and a similar tremor, and restoring the protein suppressed the tremor. Noninvasive EEG recorded over the cerebellum showed stronger rhythmic activity at tremor frequencies in patients than in controls. The mouse results suggest how misplaced synapses could contribute to tremor.

sources.citation: Pan MK et al. Sci Transl Med 12(526):eaay1769 (2020), PMID: 31941824.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two ceramic coffee mugs on a wooden table, with gentle concentric ripples across the coffee in one of them.
image.caption: In essential tremor, distal Purkinje-cell dendrites carry extra climbing-fiber synapses in parallel-fiber territory; the authors infer a pruning deficit.
